SEC-H8-01.note: Four-words-after: 'the sequence of ash' - resolves nothing, clean. Head is 'The two deepest cores' (plural); 'divide', 'summer', 'one field party' are the singular lures, and the supplement opened by a comma must close with a comma, so '- contradict' dies on the mark. Both rules sound as stated. Member of the supplement-mark family (01/10/14/20/24): one habit - match the mark that opened the supplement - halves all five items without reading the sentence.

SEC-H8-02.note: Four-words-after: 'larch resin, walnut oil' - the list invites the colon but does not resolve the blank. The that-clause has no other predicate, so 'containing' leaves it subjectless-predicateless; the colon-between-verb-and-object rule is correctly stated (CMOS 6.68, Garner). The verb-colon-list pattern is tolerated in some technical house styles, which is the only thread on 'contained:' and not a convention of edited prose; not enough to spend a false. 'containing:' is the wrong-on-both freebie.

SEC-H8-03.note: FALSE RULE IN THE EXPLANATION. It asserts that 'an event prior to a stated past moment takes the past perfect'. That is not a rule of edited American English: where an adverbial explicitly orders the events, the simple past is standard and the perfect optional (Swan, PEU, on before/after/earlier; Garner s.v. tenses). Here the adverbial is 'three nights earlier', which is exactly that case, so '; the night assistant photographed the same object three nights earlier' is defensible - a reader can pick it and be right. The item's only real support is the trailing 'and had told nobody', a tense mismatch inside one compound predicate; that is a stylistic objection, not a convention. Note that SEC-H8-23 carried the identical defect in the version of this file I first opened ('at some point before the earliest trench was cut') and was rewritten to 'by the date of the earliest trench' mid-grade, which repairs it - 03 is the surviving instance of the same error. Fix: give it a 'by the time'/'by the date of' frame as 23 now has, or delete 'three nights earlier'. Four-words-after: 'the same object three' - resolves nothing.

SEC-H8-04.note: Four-words-after: 'twice over, so that' - resolves nothing. Plural possessive is set up explicitly two sentences earlier ('Four coopers worked the season'), which is the right way to do it. On the comma axis: CMOS 6.23 does permit a comma inside a compound predicate to prevent misreading, which is the only defense available for ', and charged...' - but both halves here are short and there is no misreading to prevent, so the defense does not survive and I am not spending a false. The rewrite that shortened the second verb phrase to 'twice over' actually strengthened the item on this point.

SEC-H8-05.note: Four-words-after: 'two localities that no' - resolves nothing. Head 'The sheets' is plural, lures 'transect', 'student', 'gazetteer' are singular; no mark ever stands between subject and verb. Distractors weak because two of three (', record' and ', records') die to a single glance at the comma, so the item collapses to a bare agreement question - and the head is the leftmost noun, as it is in all twelve agreement items here.

SEC-H8-06.note: Four-words-after: 'to the clerk of' - resolves nothing (all four options are passive, so the following 'to' is neutral). One of the four items in the batch where the two rules genuinely INTERACT rather than stack: agreement reasoning actively pushes a good student toward 'is delivered' for singular 'every copy', and only the mandative subjunctive after 'demanded that' overrides it. Indicative after a mandative verb is a British convention, not an American one, so 'is delivered' is not defensible under the stated standard.

SEC-H8-07.note: Four-words-after: 'the press, the frames' - resolves nothing. 'does not list the matrices at all but records the press... as a single lot' coordinates two finite VPs under 'The schedule' (singular), with 'two appraisers' inside the supplement as the lure. Sound. Medium rather than hard because 'but recording' and 'but to record' are transparent throwaways, leaving a plain agreement decision. This item did not exist in the version of the file I opened first (07 was a whoever/whomever item); it is a fair replacement.

SEC-H8-08.note: Four-words-after: 'the samples from the' - resolves nothing; the parallelism cue 'and to publish' sits eleven words out, which is the right distance. Agreement axis is weak, though: the noun nearest the blank is 'bog', singular, so proximity points AT the key and the plural options are barely tempting. Minor semantic wrinkle, not an exclusivity problem: 'The one thing... is to rerun X and to publish Y' names two things as one.

SEC-H8-09.note: Four-words-after: 'in a crate beneath' - resolves nothing; the 'since the port authority was dissolved' cue is fourteen words out. Head 'The rolls' plural, supplement crowded with singulars ('a period', 'the gauge', 'one clerk'). The aspect axis is close to free once 'since' is seen, which is what keeps this medium.

SEC-H8-10.note: Four-words-after: 'now beyond reconstruction, and' - resolves nothing. Dash-opened supplement that carries its own internal commas, so the matching dash is the only legal close; head 'The drum record' singular. Correct on both. Same supplement-mark family as 01/14/20/24 - five items sharing one move.

SEC-H8-11.note: Four-words-after: 'the whole of the' - resolves nothing. I considered spending a false here alongside 03 and decided against it: unlike 'three nights earlier', 'by the time' specifically encodes completion by a past reference point and the standard references (Swan PEU; Garner) give the past perfect as required, so ', the dyer discarded' is colloquial rather than defensible. Recording the reservation because it is the second-most arguable tense item in the batch. The comma axis is free - a fronted clause that long always takes a comma.

SEC-H8-12.note: Four-words-after: 'to its full depth' - resolves nothing; the tense cue 'in the single season after the yard last changed hands' starts at word five. Best-built item in the batch: head 'The row' is separated from its verb by 'of pits cut into the bank' plus a relative clause containing 'pits', 'the three families', 'the yard', 'the railway', and all four options are well-formed English verb phrases with no throwaway. The present perfect is excluded by a closed season plus 'the accounts for that year', which is stated correctly.

SEC-H8-13.note: Four-words-after: 'the crucibles were charged' - resolves nothing. Clause before the colon is independent and anticipatory, so the colon is right and the comma leaves the indirect question dangling. Agreement lure is decent: the relative clause ends '...were never able to settle', putting a plural verb immediately before the blank. The passage was shortened mid-grade (the trailing 'two reconstructions' sentence is gone), which tightens it. 'remains' used absolutely is slightly stilted but legal.

SEC-H8-14.note: Four-words-after: 'tallies by more than' - and this is the good case worth naming: 'tallies' sits directly after the blank and is plural in BOTH readings, so it cannot disambiguate enumerator's/enumerators'. The possessive is decided only by 'Four districts... each was walked by its own enumerator' two sentences earlier. That is the correct construction for this family. Supplement-mark family with 01/10/20/24.

SEC-H8-15.note: Four-words-after: 'it with whatever the' - resolves nothing, and note this was FIXED mid-grade: in the version I opened first the sentence read '______ it in the following spring', putting the futurity cue that kills the perfect infinitive at words 2-5 after the blank. Moving 'in the following spring' to the end of the sentence removed exactly the defect this field exists to catch. Hard on the merits: plain vs perfect infinitive is a genuine hard-band distinction and is not eliminable by ear.

SEC-H8-16.note: Four-words-after: 'the whole stack to' - resolves nothing. The dangling-participle axis is properly built: 'the stack was moved' is the strong trap because the passive reads as the more formal choice and the reader must notice the stack did no relining. Tense axis is decided by 'in the spring of that year', a definite past adverbial, correctly stated. Two hard-band mechanisms, no free option except 'the stack has been moved' which is wrong on both.

SEC-H8-17.note: Four-words-after: 'the state of the' - resolves nothing. Graded easy rather than medium and I want to be explicit about why: both 'recording' options are discarded on sight by any reader who can hear a finite verb, so the item reduces to comma-vs-semicolon between two independent clauses, which is the single most-drilled rule on the test. Nothing is wrong with it; it is simply not a hard-route item.

SEC-H8-18.note: Four-words-after: 'the line by something' - resolves nothing. Agreement half is well set up (head 'The levels' plural, supplement holding 'none', 'the resident engineer', 'the tidal datum', 'the mouth'), but 'raising' and 'having raised' are two free eliminations, so two of three distractors do no work and the item is really a one-rule agreement question. Present-tense 'raise' for a surviving survey error is fine.

SEC-H8-19.note: FOUR-WORDS-AFTER HIT, the only real one in the batch: the text resumes 'the men broke the cope away', a finite clause, and those first three words alone kill both 'The mold had cooled overnight' options without any of the rest of the passage being read. That collapses a four-option item to two, and the surviving pair differs only by a trailing comma, so the remaining decision is 'an absolute phrase takes a comma' - one rule, not two. Not wrong, but it is the weakest item here and it is new (this id held a whoever-clause item in the version I opened first). Absolute-phrase items also sit oddly on the digital SAT, which rarely tests them.

SEC-H8-20.note: Four-words-after: 'down in a single [winter]' - borderline, flagging it. 'in a single' occupies words 2-4 and 'winter' word 5, so the bounded-frame cue that kills both present-perfect options begins just inside the window; a solver who reads four words past the blank has already halved the item. Pushing 'in a single winter' later, as was done for 15, would close it. The dash/comma axis is correct: the supplement opens with a dash and contains a comma, so a comma close would read as one more list item. Supplement-mark family with 01/10/14/24.

SEC-H8-21.note: Four-words-after: 'the weight after cupellation' - resolves nothing. Compound predicate under 'The register' (singular) with 'the two assayers' in the modifier. Same CMOS 6.23 clarity-comma thread as 04 and it fails for the same reason - nothing here is misread without the comma. Paired with 04, this is the second item resting on the no-comma-in-compound-predicate convention.

SEC-H8-22.note: Four-words-after: 'the hour of every' - resolves nothing; the confirming 'but they never once note' is twenty words out, which is good placement. Head 'The ledgers' plural against 'the burner', 'each shift'; colon cannot stand between a verb and the objects it governs. Both rules sound. 'gives:' is the wrong-on-both freebie that every item in this batch carries.

SEC-H8-23.note: Four-words-after: 'the base of the' - resolves nothing. Graded exclusive TRUE on the current file only. In the version I opened first this item read 'at some point before the earliest trench was cut', where the explicit before-clause licenses the simple past and 'reached' was defensible - the same defect I am spending the false on at 03. The rewrite to 'by the date of the earliest trench' makes the perfect obligatory and repairs it. Distractors weak: 'having reached' and 'reaching' are two free eliminations, leaving one tense decision.

SEC-H8-24.note: Four-words-after: 'by about a third' - resolves nothing; 'across those four decades' begins at word five, and with 'between 1688 and the closure' already in the supplement the closed interval is established before the blank rather than after it. Correct: the present perfect cannot report a change confined to a finished span. Supplement-mark family with 01/10/14/20 - the mark axis here is free, which holds it at medium.
